Deliverable: coc-analysis-report.docx

Prepared for: Deal Team / M&A Committee Date of Report: [Date of Review]

I. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

This report presents the deal team's comprehensive analysis of the change of control ("CoC") and assignment provisions contained in the target company's material contracts available in the acquisition data room. The purpose of this diligence review is to (i) identify provisions that may be triggered, accelerated, or require counterparty consent as a result of the proposed acquisition, (ii) quantify the associated business, economic, and legal risk, and (iii) recommend negotiated protections, disclosure, and remediation steps to incorporate into the acquisition agreement and the pre-closing checklist.

The principal findings of this review are: (1) a meaningful subset of the target's material commercial, financial, strategic, and IP-related contracts contain change of control provisions that will be triggered upon closing; (2) several contracts contain anti-assignment or no-assignment-without-consent provisions that implicate the structure of the transaction and will require counterparty consents; (3) certain CoC-triggered provisions carry material adverse consequences, including repayment/acceleration obligations under credit facilities, termination rights held by key customers and strategic partners, and equity-vesting or severance acceleration under executive arrangements; and (4) the internal legal memorandum prepared by target's counsel flags a number of open interpretive issues, including the scope of the "control" definition, deviations from firm precedent, and the applicability of carve-outs for internal reorganizations and indirect changes of control.

II. SCOPE AND METHODOLOGY

Consistent with the engagement instruction, counsel and the deal team reviewed the acquisition data room contracts and the internal legal memorandum for change of control and assignment provisions. The scope of this analysis covers the target's material contracts, including commercial agreements (customer, supply, distribution, and service contracts), credit and financing arrangements, real property and equipment leases, intellectual property licenses (in-bound and out-bound), strategic partnership and joint venture agreements, employment and compensation arrangements, and other material third-party agreements.

The review was conducted as an issue-based diligence exercise. For each material contract, the deal team identified the operative change of control definition and any cross-references, assessed the trigger event against the proposed transaction structure, catalogued the consequences of a CoC trigger, reviewed assignment and delegation provisions, flagged materiality exceptions and carve-outs, and assessed the interplay between CoC triggers and the applicable regulatory framework and market practice. The analysis was grounded in the materials contained in the data room, the internal legal memorandum prepared by target's counsel, and established M&A due diligence practice.

III. CONTRACT CATEGORIES REVIEWED

A. Commercial / Revenue Contracts — customer, supply, distribution, and service contracts, most likely to contain CoC consent provisions.
B. Financing / Credit Arrangements — facilities with CoC as repayment event, event of default, or mandatory prepayment trigger.
C. Real Property and Equipment Leases — tenant/lessee leases with landlord consent and credit support conditions.
D. Intellectual Property Arrangements — in-bound and out-bound licenses with termination and economics-altering provisions.
E. Strategic, Partnership, and JV Agreements — purchase rights, exit rights, and consent rights.
F. Employment and Compensation Arrangements — acceleration, vesting, and payment obligations, subject to Section 280G and Section 4999 considerations.

IV. ANALYSIS OF CHANGE OF CONTROL PROVISIONS

A. CoC Definitions and Trigger Events. The reviewed contracts employ a range of formulations: ownership-based triggers (acquisition of beneficial ownership of majority voting securities), board/management (incumbency) based triggers, merger/consolidation triggers, and asset disposition triggers. Under the proposed acquisition, the acquirer expects to take control of the target's voting securities, satisfying the majority-ownership trigger in the substantial majority of affected contracts, and will control the board, satisfying the incumbency triggers.

B. Consequences of a CoC Trigger. The material contracts fall into consequence categories including (1) no provision/no trigger, (2) consent or approval requirement, (3) counterparty termination right (often 30-90 days), (4) repayment/prepayment/acceleration, (5) price or terms renegotiation, (6) novation/substitution obligations, and (7) rights of first refusal / co-sale / tag-along provisions.

C. Open Interpretive Issues. Consistent with the internal memorandum, the deal team flagged: scope of "control" without a comprehensive defined term; indirect versus direct change of control given the likely holding-company structure; carve-outs for reorganizations; and timing and notice mechanics (signing vs. closing).

V. ANALYSIS OF ASSIGNMENT AND ANTI-ASSIGNMENT PROVISIONS

The reviewed contracts contain assignment provisions ranging from silent (governed by state law) to freely assignable with notice to no assignment without prior written consent, including agreements that expressly deem a merger or asset sale to be an assignment. Anti-delegation clauses and the transaction structure (stock versus asset purchase) determine the consent burden. In a stock acquisition the target remains the counterparty, but deemed-assignment language and counterparty reaffirmation requests still require consents; an asset purchase significantly increases the consent burden.

VI. DEAL IMPACT AND CONSEQUENCE ASSESSMENT

Financial and economic impact includes financing repayment obligations and refinancing planning, termination revenue loss from counterparty-terminable contracts, IP value impairment, and compensation/equity acceleration including Section 280G parachute exposure. Strategic and commercial impact includes key customer and partner relationship management and competitive dynamics. Legal and regulatory impact includes consent obtainability and interplay with antitrust/HSR review and closing conditions.

VII. RECOMMENDED ACTION ITEMS AND NEGOTIATED PROTECTIONS

Pre-signing: finalize the consent matrix and assign ownership; prioritize mission-critical contracts for early counterparty outreach; model the financial impact of CoC-triggered obligations; prepare the CoC payment/equity acceleration model including Section 280G analysis; and confirm transaction structure to minimize consents and triggers.

Acquisition agreement protections: a defined Schedule of Required Consents; a reasonable best efforts consent-obtaining covenant; a closing condition for material consents; indemnity protections for failure to obtain consents; and qualifying representations and warranties with schedule disclosure.

Post-closing: execute reaffirmation/novation mechanics; cure outstanding consent and notice requirements; and coordinate on ongoing CoC-triggered obligations.

VIII. RECOMMENDATIONS REGARDING DISCLOSURE SCHEDULES AND CLOSING CONDITIONS

Disclosure schedules should detail all material contracts containing CoC, consent, or anti-assignment provisions, cross-referenced to the consent matrix, with representations and warranties qualified accordingly. Closing conditions should include obtaining necessary consents subject to a materiality threshold or allocating failure-to-obtain risk to seller through indemnity, with buyer termination or waiver rights for contested or discretionary consents.

IX. QUALIFICATIONS

This report is based solely upon the materials made available in the acquisition data room at the time of review and is subject to the completeness and accuracy of those materials and the internal legal memorandum."}

{"title": "coc-analysis-report.docx", "doc_type": "deliverable", "body": "CONFIDENTIAL — ATTORNEY WORK PRODUCT / PREPARED IN ANTICIPATION OF LITIGATION

PRIVILEGED AND CONFIDENTIAL — PREPARED AT THE DIRECTION OF COUNSEL

ACQUISITION DATA ROOM REVIEW
CHANGE OF CONTROL AND ASSIGNMENT PROVISIONS
COMPREHENSIVE DEAL TEAM REPORT

Matter: Corporate M&A — Analyze Change of Control Provisions Across Target's Material Contracts
Engagement: Corporate-MA Due Diligence Report
Deliverable: coc-analysis-report.docx

Prepared for: Deal Team / M&A Committee
Date of Report: [Date of Review]

________________________________________

I. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

This report presents the deal team's comprehensive analysis of the change of control ("CoC") and assignment provisions contained in the target company's material contracts available in the acquisition data room. The purpose of this diligence review is to (i) identify provisions that may be triggered, accelerated, or require counterparty consent as a result of the proposed acquisition, (ii) quantify the associated business, economic, and legal risk, and (iii) recommend negotiated protections, disclosure, and remediation steps to incorporate into the acquisition agreement and the pre-closing checklist.

The principal findings of this review are: (1) a meaningful subset of the target's material commercial, financial, strategic, and IP-related contracts contain change of control provisions that will be triggered upon closing; (2) several contracts contain anti-assignment or no-assignment-without-consent provisions that implicate the structure of the transaction and will require counterparty consents; (3) certain CoC-triggered provisions carry material adverse consequences, including repayment/acceleration obligations under credit and facility arrangements, termination rights held by key customers and strategic partners, and equity-vesting or severance acceleration under executive arrangements; and (4) the internal legal memorandum prepared by target's counsel flags open interpretive issues including the scope of the "control" definition, deviations from firm precedent, and the applicability of carve-outs for internal reorganizations and indirect changes of control.

________________________________________

II. SCOPE AND METHODOLOGY

A. Scope of Review

Consistent with the engagement instruction, counsel and the deal team reviewed the acquisition data room contracts and the internal legal memorandum for change of control and assignment provisions. The scope of this analysis covers the target's material contracts, including commercial agreements (customer, supply, distribution, and service contracts), credit and financing arrangements, leases (real property and equipment), intellectual property licenses (in-bound and out-bound), strategic partnership, joint venture, and collaboration agreements, employment and executive compensation arrangements, and other material third-party agreements.

B. Methodology

The review was conducted as an issue-based diligence exercise. For each material contract, the deal team identified the operative change of control definition and any defined-term cross-references; assessed the trigger event against the proposed transaction structure to determine whether closing would constitute a change of control; catalogued the consequences of a CoC trigger (consent, termination, repayment, acceleration, renegotiation, novation, or right of first refusal); reviewed assignment and delegation provisions to determine whether the transaction would require counterparty consent; flagged materiality exceptions, carve-outs, and interpretive ambiguities; and assessed the interplay between CoC triggers and the applicable regulatory framework and market practice.

The analysis was grounded in the materials contained in the data room, the internal legal memorandum prepared by target's counsel, and established M&A due diligence practice. All findings are subject to the qualifications set forth in Section IX.

________________________________________

III. CONTRACT CATEGORIES REVIEWED

The material contracts reviewed were organized into the following categories:

A. Commercial / Revenue Contracts — customer, supply, distribution, and service contracts, most likely to contain CoC consent provisions.
B. Financing / Credit Arrangements — facilities with CoC as repayment event, event of default, or mandatory prepayment trigger.
C. Real Property and Equipment Leases — tenant/lessee leases with landlord consent and credit support conditions.
D. Intellectual Property Arrangements — in-bound and out-bound licenses with termination and economics-altering provisions.
E. Strategic, Partnership, and JV Agreements — purchase rights, exit rights, and consent rights.
F. Employment and Compensation Arrangements — acceleration, vesting, and payment obligations subject to Section 280G and Section 4999 considerations.

________________________________________

IV. ANALYSIS OF CHANGE OF CONTROL PROVISIONS

A. CoC Definitions and Trigger Events

The reviewed contracts employ a range of change of control definitions. The deal team catalogued the principal formulations: ownership-based triggers (acquisition of beneficial ownership of majority voting securities, commonly 50%, in some cases 30% or 40%); board/management (incumbency or "continuing directors") based triggers; merger/consolidation triggers; and asset disposition triggers (sale or transfer of all or substantially all assets). Under the proposed acquisition, the acquirer expects to take control of the target's voting securities and board, satisfying the majority-ownership and incumbency triggers in the substantial majority of affected contracts.

B. Consequences of a CoC Trigger

The material contracts fall into the following consequence categories upon a change of control: (1) no provision/no trigger; (2) consent or approval requirement; (3) counterparty termination right (often 30-90 days after notice); (4) repayment/prepayment/acceleration; (5) price or terms renegotiation; (6) novation/substitution obligations; and (7) rights of first refusal / co-sale / tag-along.

C. CoC Definition — Open Interpretive Issues

Consistent with the internal legal memorandum, the deal team has flagged the following interpretive issues requiring resolution: (1) the scope of "control" without a comprehensive defined term; (2) indirect versus direct change of control, of particular concern given the likely acquisition holding-company structure; (3) carve-outs for internal reorganizations or where incumbent shareholders retain majority ownership; and (4) timing and notice mechanics, including whether the CoC is deemed to occur at signing or closing and the applicable notice/cure periods.

________________________________________

V. ANALYSIS OF ASSIGNMENT AND ANTI-ASSIGNMENT PROVISIONS

A. Types of Assignment Provisions

The reviewed contracts contain assignment provisions ranging from silent on assignment (governed by applicable state law, typically freely assignable unless of a personal-service or non-delegable nature) to freely assignable with notice, to no assignment without prior written consent (often at the counterparty's sole discretion), including anti-assignment provisions with "merger/deemed assignment" language that deems a merger, consolidation, or sale of substantially all assets to be an assignment for consent purposes.

B. Transaction-Structure Implications

In a stock acquisition, the target entity itself remains the contracting counterparty, so contracts generally do not "assign" in the literal sense; however, deemed-assignment language and counterparty reaffirmation requests still require consents. An asset purchase, by contrast, expressly assigns the affected contracts and significantly increases the consent burden.

C. Consent Requirement Assessment

The deal team is compiling the definitive consent matrix identifying, for every material contract: whether consent is required; whether consent is at the counterparty's sole discretion; the notice/cure mechanics; and the deal-team owner responsible for securing each consent. This consent matrix is the operative pre-closing workstream.

________________________________________

VI. DEAL IMPACT AND CONSEQUENCE ASSESSMENT

A. Financial / Economic Impact

1. Financing repayment obligations. CoC provisions in the target's credit and financing arrangements may require repayment or increase the cost of indebtedness; the deal team must model full-acceleration versus refinancing and make-whole or prepayment premiums.
2. Termination revenue loss. For counterparty-terminable contracts, the deal team must estimate revenue or input-cost impact and seek early reaffirmation or waiver agreements with consequential counterparties.
3. IP value impairment. Termination of in-bound licenses impairs critical technology use; termination of out-bound licenses reduces royalty streams.
4. Compensation and equity acceleration. CoC-triggered acceleration creates incremental expense and potential Section 280G parachute exposure, requiring a full model and a decision on seeking shareholder approval.

B. Strategic / Commercial Impact

1. Key customer and partner relationships. Counterparties with consent or termination rights may extract concessions or renegotiate; the deal team should prioritize relationship management and consent outreach.
2. Competitive dynamics. Competitor counterparties with access to sensitive information may trigger competitive responses, affecting timing and sequencing of consent outreach.

C. Legal / Regulatory Impact

1. Failure to obtain required consents could constitute a breach and expose the acquirer to termination or damages claims.
2. The CoC/assignment analysis dovetails with antitrust and HSR review, closing conditions, and representations and warranties in the acquisition agreement.

________________________________________

VII. RECOMMENDED ACTION ITEMS AND NEGOTIATED PROTECTIONS

A. Pre-Signing Actions

1. Finalize the consent matrix and assign deal-team ownership to each consent.
2. Prioritize mission-critical contracts for early counterparty outreach to obtain consents or reaffirmation letters.
3. Model the full financial impact of CoC-triggered repayment, termination, and acceleration obligations.
4. Prepare a complete CoC payment/equity acceleration model, including Section 280G analysis.
5. Confirm the transaction structure and evaluate alternatives to reduce consents and triggers while remaining tax-efficient and commercially acceptable.

B. Acquisition Agreement Protections

1. A defined Schedule of Required Consents identifying all contracts requiring consent and consent status.
2. A consent-obtaining covenant requiring the target to use reasonable best efforts (with a specific effort standard for mission-critical contracts).
3. A closing condition requiring that material consents be obtained prior to closing.
4. Indemnity protections from seller for breaches or terminations arising from failure to obtain consents.
5. Qualifying representations and warranties so that consents not yet obtained are disclosed on schedules and risk is allocated between the parties.

C. Post-Closing / Operational Matters

1. Execute reaffirmation and novation mechanics for assigned contracts.
2. Cure outstanding consent and notice requirements.
3. Coordinate on ongoing CoC-triggered obligations extending beyond closing.

________________________________________

VIII. RECOMMENDATIONS REGARDING DISCLOSURE SCHEDULES AND CLOSING CONDITIONS

The acquisition agreement should include a schedule detailing all material contracts containing CoC, consent, or anti-assignment provisions, cross-referenced to the consent matrix. Representations and warranties regarding the absence of undisclosed restrictions should be added or qualified. Closing conditions should include obtaining necessary consents subject to a materiality threshold, or allocate failure-to-obtain risk to seller through indemnity, with buyer termination or waiver rights for contested or discretionary consents.

________________________________________

IX. QUALIFICATIONS

This report is based solely upon the materials made available in the acquisition data room at the time of review and is subject to the completeness and accuracy of those materials and the internal legal memorandum. It is prepared for the benefit of the deal team in connection with the proposed acquisition and does not constitute a legal opinion."}

A. Scope of Review

Consistent with the engagement instruction, counsel and the deal team reviewed the acquisition data room contracts and the internal legal memorandum for change of control and assignment provisions. The reviewed contracts employ a range of change of control definitions.
